---
title: "How to Play Congas: Five Strokes and the Tumbao"
toc: true
toc-depth: 2
---

This is a first lesson for someone who has never played congas. You will learn five ways
to strike the drum, how they are written, and the most common conga part there is, the
**tumbao**. You need one drum. If you have no drum yet you can still follow the notation and
listen to the band play each step.

**How to use the page.** Every step has two bars of the part written large, a chord chart,
and the whole chorus written on a conga staff. The note that is sounding lights up in the
notation as the band plays. Press ▶ and the band plays it; the bar that is sounding lights up
on the chart. Tick **Congas alone** to hear the congas without the bass and piano, and
**Leave out the congas** to play them yourself. Each step starts in its own style and tempo;
the strip at the bottom changes both.

**About the sounds.** The sounds on this page are General MIDI stand-ins. The computer has only
an open tone, a muted tone and a low drum, so the heel, toe, slap and bass tones you hear here
are approximations. Listen to a real player for the sound.

## The drums

The **conga** is the higher drum of a pair, and the one this lesson uses. The **tumba** is the
lower drum. A conga player often has both, and step 6 uses the tumba for a moment; everything
else on this page is played on one drum.

## Sitting and hands

This is ordinary advice, not a method. Sit upright, near the front of the chair, with the drum
between your knees. Tilt it slightly away from you, or put it on a stand, so the bottom is open
and the sound can come out. Keep your wrists and hands loose: a tight hand makes a dead sound
and tires quickly. Take rings off. If anything hurts, stop and rest; a drum head is hard, and
a beginner's hands need time.

## The five strokes

The names and the first description of each stroke are from the teacher's handout. Each button
plays the stroke.

**Bass tone** <button type="button" class="btn btn-sm btn-outline-secondary" data-conga-hit="congaBass">▶ Hear it</button><br>
Strike the center of the head with the palm of the hand. It is the lowest sound the drum makes.

**Open tone** <button type="button" class="btn btn-sm btn-outline-secondary" data-conga-hit="congaOpen">▶ Hear it</button><br>
Strike near the edge of the head with the base of your fingers. Use the first four fingers at
the edge and let them bounce off, so that the drum rings.

**Muted tone** <button type="button" class="btn btn-sm btn-outline-secondary" data-conga-hit="congaMute">▶ Hear it</button><br>
Strike the center of the head with the palm of the hand, creating a deep tone. Teachers differ on
this name. Some say "muffled", and some mean a tone where the fingers stay on the head after the
strike. The handout's description is the one used on this page.

**Slap tone** <button type="button" class="btn btn-sm btn-outline-secondary" data-conga-hit="congaSlap">▶ Hear it</button><br>
Strike the edge of the head with flat fingertips to create a high, pinging sound. The slap is
the hardest stroke to learn and takes time. Do not expect it to ring on the first day.

**Heel-toe** <button type="button" class="btn btn-sm btn-outline-secondary" data-conga-hit="congaHeel">▶ Hear it</button><br>
Strike the center of the head with the heel of the palm, then rock forward to slap with the
fingers. It is a rocking motion of the hand: first the heel, then the fingertips. It is a quiet
stroke, used as filler between the louder ones. On this page the two halves are written as two
notes, **heel** and **toe**.

## Reading a conga part

Click a note head to hear that stroke. The conga is written on the top space of the staff. The
head says how it is struck: a plain head for the open tone and the bass tone, an ✕ for the slap,
a triangle for the heel and the toe, and a diamond for the muted tone. The open tone and the
bass tone look the same, so read the letter.

<div class="bl-congakey"></div>

In a part, two lines of words sit under the notes. The first line is the stroke: **H** heel,
**T** toe, **S** slap, **O** open, **M** muted, **B** bass. The second line is the hand: **L**
left and **R** right. A left-handed player can reverse the hands. A low drum, when there is one,
is written on a lower space.

## 1. The two notes everyone hears

The tumbao is built up from the end of the bar. Start with the two open tones, on **4** and the
**and of 4**. Count "1 and 2 and 3 and 4 and" and play only on the last two. Use the right hand
for both, one after the other.

<div class="bl-step" data-part="opens" data-chart="vamp"></div>

These are the two notes a listener notices. When they come in the right place, the rest of
the part has somewhere to go.

## 2. The right hand

Now add the **slap on 2**. The right hand plays all of it: the slap on 2, then the two open
tones on 4 and the and of 4. Between them the right hand rests, and you keep counting.

<div class="bl-step" data-part="righthand" data-chart="vamp"></div>

If the slap will not come, play it as an open tone for now and come back to it. Take it slowly.

## 3. The left hand

Put the right hand away and play the other half. The left hand plays **heel** on 1, **toe** on
the and of 1, **toe** on the and of 2, **heel** on 3 and **toe** on the and of 3. It is the
rocking heel-toe stroke, quiet. The gaps left in the bar are where the right hand will go.

<div class="bl-step" data-part="lefthand" data-chart="vamp"></div>

## 4. Both hands, slowly

Put the two hands together. The strokes in order are **Heel Toe Slap Toe Heel Toe Open Open**,
and the hands are **L L R L L L R R**. The left hand plays every quiet heel and toe; the right hand plays
the slap and the two open tones. This is the tumbao, as the handout writes it: a pattern of
heel-toe-slap-toe figures and a pair of open tones. The sticking is the one given for the tumbao
by Rebeca Mauleón in *Salsa Guidebook*, as quoted in the Wikipedia article on the tumbao.

<div class="bl-step" data-part="tumbao" data-chart="vamp"></div>

This step is slow, and the band has no drummer, so the congas are easy to hear. Loop it and
play along until your hands do not argue.

## 5. With a band

The same part in the Cha-cha, at a moderate tempo, with the drummer in. The tumbao is the most
common pattern on congas and bongos, and it fits cha-cha, son and boogaloo. The Feel menu at the
bottom plays it in the other two.

<div class="bl-step" data-part="chacha" data-chart="vamp"></div>

Listen for the **clave** in the other instruments: a rhythm of five notes over two bars,
three in one bar and two in the other, that the whole band is built around. You do not need to
play it to play the tumbao, but it explains the next step.

## 6. Two drums

Players who have two drums use the second one in the tumbao. Here, in Son montuno, every second
bar the right hand plays two open tones on the **low drum**, on the **and of 2** and on **3**,
in place of the toe and the heel. It is the bar with three clave notes (the second bar of a 2-3
clave, as Mauleón's book has it, again via the Wikipedia article). Look at the two bars written
large: the second has the notes on a lower space.

<div class="bl-step" data-part="twodrums" data-chart="vamp"></div>

Stay on one drum until step 5 is easy. The two-drum bar is an extra, not a part of the basic
tumbao.

## Where to go next

- Play step 5 with **Leave out the congas** ticked for ten choruses without losing the beat.
- Take the tumbao to a tune: [Watermelon Man for Congas](watermelon-congas.qmd) plays it in a
  16-bar blues.
- **Tools → Backing Track** has a Congas menu that works in any style: put a tumbao under a tune
  you know.
- Listen to a real conga player and copy what you hear. A page cannot give you the sound of the
  hands.
